To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

peptides which compete with the presentation of Pc by APC do not share a single biochemical property and that peptides with stable α‐helices show greater blocking activity than the equivalent linear peptide, suggesting that α‐helical structure contributes to the blocking ability of the peptide.

the ability of a synthetic peptide to compete with a globular protein antigen for binding sites at the APC surface does not depend on the amino acid sequence, secondary structure or major histocompatibility class of the peptide.
peptides of diverse physiochemical properties can block the presentation of antigen by APC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the biochemical characteristics of peptides which compete with the presented antigen for binding to the APC.
understanding the mechanisms by which the immune system recognizes foreign proteins and generates a response against them.
the mechanism by which APC present protein antigens for recognition by T cell receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no single biochemical property, amino acid sequence, or algorithm predicts the ability of a given peptide to block the presentation of Pc by APC.
the peptides which block the presentation of Pc are those peptides which bind to the APC surface with sufficient affinity to compete with the presented Pc.
the ability of peptides to compete for presented Pc is dependent on the amino acid composition of the peptides, the length of the peptides, and the secondary structure of the peptides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability of peptides to block presentation of antigen by APC is a property of the peptide itself, and is not related to the physicochemical properties of the antigen from which it is derived.

peptides which compete for the antigen‐presenting sites of APC are not predicted to adopt a stable amphipathic secondary structure and are not predicted by their amino acid sequence or by the major histocompatibilty complex restriction of their T cell epitopes.
the peptides which block presentation of Pc are not predicted by any single property or algorithm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the peptides which block the presented Pc are not restricted to any particular physiochemical properties or amino acid sequence.
the peptides which compete with the presentation of Pc are not predicted by any single algorithm.
the ability to block the presentation of a protein antigen is not predicted by any single physicochemical property of the peptide, nor is it predicted by the amino acid sequence.
